# Assessing the effectiveness of building retrofits in reducing GHG emissions: A Canadian school case study
Felipe Grossi [a](#page-0-0) , Hua Ge [a](#page-0-0), [*](#page-0-1) , Radu Zmeureanu [a](#page-0-0) , Fuad Baba [b](#page-0-2)

#### ARTICLE INFO
#### *Keywords:* Whole building life cycle analysis Life cycle assessment Embodied emissions
Operational emissions Building energy retrofits Electricity grid profile Carbon neutrality
#### ABSTRACT
This paper investigates the impact of energy retrofits on life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions across different electricity grid profiles in Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, using an existing school building as a case study. Using DesignBuilder for energy simulations and OneClick LCA for GHG emissions estimation, this study evaluates whether the reduction in the operational emission achieved by energy savings from retrofits can outweigh the increased embodied emissions from new envelope materials and equipment. In Montreal and Ottawa, where electricity is mainly generated from renewables and non-fossil fuels, retrofits involving electric heating and envelope improvements could decrease life cycle GHG emissions by up to 75 %. However, if the building initially used electric heating, the retrofits led to an increase in life cycle carbon emissions by 170 % in Montreal and 56 % in Ottawa, respectively, due to the embodied emissions of retrofit materials and equipment. In Halifax, where the electricity grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, all retrofit scenarios showed a positive impact on GHG reductions. Enhancing the building envelope and transitioning from natural gas to electric heating slightly reduced total emissions by 4 %, but retaining natural gas heating decreased the total life cycle GHG emissions by 27 %. This study emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive life cycle assessment in developing policies for achieving carbon neutrality. It demonstrates that the effectiveness of retrofits in reducing GHG emissions significantly depends on the local energy grid, suggesting tailored approaches based on regional energy profiles to optimize emission reductions and energy efficiency.
## **1.** **Introduction**
The extensive consumption of energy, notably from fossil fuels, plays a significant role in influencing climate change (P.S. and P.C. Government of [[1,](#page-14-0)[2](#page-14-1)]). The building and construction sector contributed around 37 % of the total CO^(2) emissions and one-third of global energy consumption [[3]](#page-14-2). Since 28 % of CO^(2) emissions are generated from the operational emissions in the buildings, including the energy from electricity, natural gas, and refrigerant, and 11 % due to materials and construction processes (embodied emissions) ([[4](#page-14-3)]9), most of the previous studies focus on operational emissions. For example, Cuéllar-Franca and Azapagic [[5](#page-14-4)], Asdrubali et al. [[6](#page-14-5)], and Chastas et al. [[7]](#page-14-6) highlighted that buildings contribute at least 80–90 % of CO^(2) emissions during their use phase, while around 10–20 % of CO^(2) emissions occur during the construction phase.
To reduce operational energy consumption and carbon emission, many countries have implemented new building standards aimed at achieving net-zero energy buildings [[1,](#page-14-0)8–[10]](#page-14-7). In addition, new energy laws are being introduced to reduce the carbon inten-

Ramesh et al. [[14](#page-14-11)] and Gustavsson and Joelsson [[15]](#page-14-12) found that in buildings with low energy efficiency, the embodied emissions contributed by 10 %–20 % to total emissions, while in buildings with high energy efficiency, this value can reach about 45 %. Paleari et al. [[16]](#page-14-13) and Dodoo et al. [[17]](#page-14-14) discovered that in highly energy-efficient buildings, the proportion of embodied emissions can exceed 60 %. Therefore, in the last decade, the environmental impacts associated with embodied emissions in materials and equipment throughout a building's life cycle have become increasingly significant and should not be overlooked, especially with NZEBs [[18](#page-14-15)–20]. Also, a new awareness of accounting for whole building life cycle carbon emissions has motivated the construction industry to develop Net-Zero Carbon Buildings (ZCB) [[19](#page-14-16),[21,](#page-14-17)[22]](#page-14-18), also referred to as Carbon Neutral Buildings. Carbon Neutral Buildings are highly efficient buildings, operated using 100 % fossil-free energy and designed following the "best practice sustainable construction" [[21](#page-14-17)]. This term stands for a number of strategies to reduce carbon emissions in buildings, such as promoting energy savings and well-being of occupants through passive design, maximizing the use of recycled and nature-based materials, minimizing energy use in all stages of the building's life, and creating new green spaces [[22]](#page-14-18).
With the growing emphasis on sustainable development, the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) technique has gained importance in architectural and engineering practices. LCA can be used to evaluate the environmental impact of a building across its entire life cycle, guiding informed decision-making on design solutions that can enhance a building's environmental performance. In 2023, the term "Whole Building Life-Cycle Assessments (WBLCAs)", which was adopted from European Standards 15978:2011 and 15643, was developed [[23](#page-14-19)]. The WBLCAs are a framework that allows for the assessment of the environmental impacts from all life-cycle stages of a building, including embodied and operational impacts [[23]](#page-14-19). Brooks et al. [[24]](#page-14-20) analyzed the operational emissions and the embodied carbon life cycle (LCA) of an old residential building in the UK, and they evaluated the impact of low carbon and clean technologies on reducing embodied and operational carbon using the 'cradle-to-grave' process. They found that the use of photovoltaic panels to reduce operational emissions, and the use of recycled steel, lightweight brick, and Supplementary Cementing Material (SCM) for mortar and concrete reduced overall CO^(2) emissions by 22 % [[24]](#page-14-20). Asdrubali and Grazieschi [[25](#page-14-21)] conducted a study to assess the potential reduction of both operational and embodied emissions by retrofitting old buildings in Italy. Their findings indicate that retrofitting an old building to a net-zero energy building leads to a substantial reduction in operational emissions, with a maximum decrease of 89 %. However, when considering embodied emissions from added materials, which include organic fossil insulation materials (EPS), new windows, photovoltaic panels, and solar thermal systems, the maximum reduction achieved by the reduction in the operational emissions will decrease to 48 % [[25]](#page-14-21).
In net-zero energy buildings (NZEBs), not only do embodied emissions emerge as a crucial factor in LCA, but also the presence of electricity mix systems within NZEBs necessitates the utilization of Dynamic LCA (DLCA) methodologies. Dynamic LCA allows for consideration of temporal changes and is defined as ''an approach to LCA which explicitly incorporates dynamic process modelling in the context of temporal and spatial variations in the surrounding industrial and environmental systems" [[26]](#page-14-22). The utilization of onsite renewable energy generation for electricity production experiences temporal changes. For instance, photovoltaic (PV) systems generate electricity during daylight hours but are inactive at night. Additionally, substantial variations occur seasonally, with increased production during the summer months and decreased generation in winter, therefore, Dynamic LCA became necessary [[27](#page-14-23)]. Also, Dynamic LCA is used to evaluate the impact of future years on the LCA during the lifetime of the buildings [[28,](#page-14-24)[29](#page-14-25)]. Goldstein et al. [[30](#page-14-26)] discovered that occupant consumption patterns and socioeconomic variances can impact the evaluation of LCA for buildings, emphasizing the importance of employing Dynamic LCA for WBLCA. Ramon et al. [[31]](#page-14-27) evaluated the potential changes in operational emissions use due to climate change in Belgian office buildings. They found that with the Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 scenario, the annual heating consumption will reduce by 18 % but the cooling consumption will increase by 34 %. They additionally assessed the impact of the electricity mix, representing the blend of energy sources (both renewable and fossil fuels) utilized for electricity generation within a specific region over time, as a strategy for climate change mitigation compared to static electricity, where the energy source remains fixed over time. They found that the CO^(2) emissions of the office building will be reduced by 13 % for an electricity mix dominated by renewable electrical generation (56 %), but increased by 10 % for an electricity mix dominated by gas.
Despite the great number of studies addressing building LCA and low-carbon design strategies, there is still no consensus on the strategy for large-scale implementation of carbon-neutral buildings. While progress has been made toward designing and constructing carbon-neutral buildings, comprehensive case studies that cover the full range of building components and life cycle stages are relatively scarce in the literature. Most LCA studies present an incomplete scope, usually overlooking the impacts of embodied emissions from mechanical equipment, Photovoltaic (PV) panels, internal partitions, and finishes. Several case studies that implement low-carbon strategies to attempt for carbon-neutral building status have been identified. The low-carbon strategies include highperformance building envelopes such as high-value thermal resistance, triple-pane windows, airtightness, bio-based building materials, air-source or geothermal heat pump systems, hybrid PV and solar thermal systems, green roofs or green areas surrounding buildings. All case studies cover energy efficiency analysis, while the scope of carbon emission analysis is primarily on the embodied carbon in structural and building envelope materials with some including the carbon sequestration of greenery over the building's service life. These case studies were chosen because they are real-case existing buildings and provided details about design solutions, materials, software used, building's carbon footprint, and energy use.
The report from Humber College [[32](#page-14-28)] showcases the achievement of Zero Carbon Building (ZCB)-Design certification through a building retrofit project in Toronto, Canada. The retrofit included envelope improvements, mechanical system upgrades, lighting enhancements, and the installation of a PV system. The 5-storey building of about 4500 m^(2) was designed to achieve an Energy Use Intensity (EUI) of 63 kWh/m^(2) ∙year, which corresponds to a 70 % reduction in energy use compared to existing institutional buildings.
The embodied carbon emissions, of new and existing building materials, were estimated at 377.4 kgCO2eq/m^(2) of floor area. However, the embodied emissions related to HVAC and PV systems were not included.
Dabaieh et al. [[33](#page-14-29)[,34](#page-14-30)] assessed the environmental impacts of a Swedish experimental house over 15 years. They incorporated passive systems to reduce cooling and heating loads (i.e. earth air heat exchanger; Trombe wall, and green walls), used bio-based construction materials (i.e. compressed straw panels, wood fiberboards, wood-fiber insulation, cross-laminated timber), and integrated renewable energy systems (hybrid solar PV and wind power systems, solar water heater, and biogas tank using organic waste for cooking and domestic hot water). The energy simulations showed a 33 % reduction in energy consumption than the reference house. The life cycle assessment showed that plant-based materials can drastically reduce the carbon footprint. When the sequestration capacity of plants (green walls) and storage in plant-based materials are considered, the overall Global Warming Potential (GWP) is reduced by 226.2 kgCO2eq/m^(2) . Otherwise, the GWP was increased by 254.7 kgCO2eq/m^(2) over a 15-year period compared to the reference Swedish house. The embodied emissions of PV panels and wind turbines were not considered in the LCA analysis.
Bhavsar et al. [[35](#page-14-31)] analyzed a new educational facility at Mohawk College, Canada. The walls, roof, and windows have higher thermal resistance than the Ontario Building Code. The building was designed to generate 100 % of its end-use energy by using an onsite PV system for electricity generation, a geothermal system for heating and cooling, and a solar thermal system for domestic hot water. Other low-carbon solutions included the use of steel with highly recyclable contents, concrete mix with Supplementary Cementing Material (SCM) content (such as slag), a cistern for rainwater harvesting, low-flush urinals in toilets, and low-flow faucets. The cradle-to-grave LCA analysis of the building structure over a 60-year period was performed, however, other carbon-intensive components such as windows, insulation, mechanical equipment, and PV systems were not included.
Similarly, LCA studies on the Evolv office building [[36](#page-15-0)] in Canada, which was certified under the CaGBC Zero Carbon Building Standard with embodied emissions due to the envelope and structural materials estimated at 260 kgCO2eq/m^(2) , and a dwelling in Taiwan [[37]](#page-15-1) also did not include HVAC and PV systems in their analysis.
The incomplete scope of many LCA studies can potentially introduce biased benchmarking and restrict our understanding of the effectiveness of building decarbonization strategies. In the context of energy efficiency and retrofit design solutions for carbonneutral buildings, this paper presents a complete LCA analysis approach coupling energy efficiency, operational and embodied carbon emission, and the regional electricity grid profile that architects and engineers may consider, along with policymakers, when conducting the environmental impact assessment of a building. This approach addresses the incompleteness in LCA impact analysis, i.e. incomplete building systems, and incomplete life cycle stages, and introduces the connection between buildings and the electricity grid. This is the novelty of this paper.
The objective of this study is to develop a holistic approach to evaluate the effectiveness of retrofitting strategies in achieving carbon-neutral building status through life cycle carbon emission analysis within the context of local electricity grid profiles to assist building designers and policymakers in retrofitting decision-making from life cycle carbon emission perspective. This approach is applied to a 2-storey natural gas-heated school building as a case study to test the hypothesis that those building retrofit measures that reduce the energy use for heating might not always reduce the building's greenhouse gas (GHG) emission during its life cycle depending on the local electricity-grid profile. The impact of local grid profile on buildings' environmental performance is assessed for three cities, Montreal (Quebec), Ottawa (Ontario), and Halifax (Nova Scotia), having similar climatic characteristics but different electricity grid profiles. Few studies have been reported in the literature, especially within the Canadian context, for such a complete life cycle carbon analysis. This study attempts to fill this gap and contribute to advancing the large-scale realization of carbon-neutral buildings.
#### **2.** **Methodology**
The approach described in this paper demonstrates the process of assessing the environmental performance of building retrofits, using energy simulation and life cycle assessment (LCA). Energy simulation is employed to estimate the potential reduction of annual energy consumption when introducing different improvements, such as adding thermal insulation, replacing windows, and adding exterior shading. On the other hand, LCA estimates the embodied emissions associated with the manufacture of each new envelope or HVAC component, as well as the reduction of operational emissions resulting from the energy efficiency improvements. This holistic overall system analysis provides a more complete picture for retrofitting from a life cycle carbon emission perspective.
## *2.1.* *Overview*
The process began with an analysis of the existing school building located in Montreal, which served as the baseline. An energy model was developed using DesignBuilder (EnergyPlus) (v7.0.2.006) [[38](#page-15-2)]to simulate the building's annual energy use. Following the simulation for the original design, the model was refined to incorporate each retrofit improvement, and the new annual energy use was calculated at each step. The data on annual energy use obtained from DesignBuilder (EnergyPlus) served as one of the inputs for calculating the building's operational CO^(2) emissions. The calculation of both embodied and operational emissions was carried out using OneClick LCA [[39]](#page-15-3), which is an automated LCA tool designed to estimate the carbon footprint of buildings and infrastructure.
After using the energy simulation results from DesignBuilder (EnergyPlus) to calculate operational emissions in OneClick LCA, the next step involved the calculation of embodied emissions. A list of materials organized by building assembly was mapped into OneClick LCA software, with each item linked to an inventory data point. The software's datasets are customized regionally, accounting for factors such as local electricity grids and material options specific to the building's location. When necessary, information regarding thickness, density, and other material properties was also provided.
SimaPro, Sophera (GaBi), and OneClick LCA are different examples of LCA tools. The choice between these softwares often depends on the specific requirements of the LCA study and the availability of relevant databases. SimaPro (2022) [[40](#page-15-4)] and GaBi (2024) [[41]](#page-15-5) are process-based softwares that allow users to create the life cycle of a product based on inputs such as raw materials, extraction methods, transportation modes, and processing methods. In this study, we looked for an LCA tool that could provide product-ready inputs to represent an entire building. OneClick LCA was selected for being an automated, cloud-based software that offers simplified LCA workflows for buildings and infrastructure. The software uses third-party-verified industry-available data, such as Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) from various manufacturers to create material options that can be put together to estimate the environmental impacts of an entire building over a defined calculation period. Other commonly used LCA tools include the Athena Impact Estimator for Buildings [[42]](#page-15-6), which allows users to input a bill of materials or quickly describe building assemblies through dialogue boxes. The software then calculates a bill of materials with associated environmental impacts. A comparison between LCA results provided by Athena and OneClick LCA for a different building can be found in our previous study, Grossi et al. [[43](#page-15-7)].
The LCA results presented in this paper were estimated from cradle-to-grave over a 20-year calculation period. The choice of the 20-year calculation period is to avoid the incidence of secondary emissions resulting from subsequent replacements of building components and systems. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate the advantages or disadvantages of a single retrofit event occurring at different Canadian locations. In addition, adopting a shorter calculation period reduces the uncertainties related to future energy profiles and technological development, which are key factors influencing LCA estimation outcomes. Given that many LCA standards recommend a 60-year timeframe, we have also included a scenario considering the heat pump COP of 2.0 over a 60-year period for comparison, and results are presented in section [3.5](#page-11-0).
The case study building is located in Montreal (Quebec). To investigate the influence of local electricity-grid profiles on the building's environmental performance, the same process was applied to Ottawa (Ontario), and Halifax (Nova Scotia), using the corresponding weather files and electricity-grid profiles.
## *2.2.* *Case* *study* *building* *and* *retrofit* *measures*
The baseline of this study is a 2-story school building with a total heated floor area of 2300 m^(2) . The exterior walls are composed of brick veneer on the outside, followed by a 25 mm air gap, 70 mm of mineral wool (MW) insulation, Concrete Masonry Units, and gypsum plaster on the inner layer. The roof consists of a waterproof roofing membrane, fiberboard, 130 mm of XPS insulation, and a 100 mm concrete slab. The windows are double (clear) glazing with a 13 mm air gap. As many other schools built in the past, the building does not have a cooling system and mechanical ventilation. More information about the baseline building can be found in Ref. [[44](#page-15-8)].
Five retrofitting improvements are implemented sequentially, as shown in [Fig.](#page-3-0) 1. The first improvement consists of replacing the natural gas heating system with a thermal efficiency of 0.75 with an electric heating system with a Coefficient of Performance (COP) of 1 while maintaining all other components such as insulation and windows in their original condition. An electrical baseboard is a commonly used heating system in Quebec. The next step consists of increasing the thermal insulation of the roof and exterior walls to meet the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings [[45](#page-15-9)] requirements. Then, the building envelope airtightness is increased from 3.9 ACH to 2.0 ACH at 50 Pa as input in the energy model to reflect post-retrofit conditions by adding a new roofing membrane and air barriers as necessary to reduce the air infiltration rate through the building envelope. The subsequent step consists of upgrading windows and interior blinds, and the installation of overhangs. The addition of blinds and overhangs is to address the summer overheating issue [[46]](#page-15-10). Finally, a mechanical ventilation system is added to ensure the supply of minimum ventilation air (as required by NECB), followed by the installation of a heat recovery ventilator from the exhaust air with a heat transfer effectiveness of 0.7.

To investigate the impact of local electricity grid profile on a building's environmental performance, we have selected three Canadian cities: Montreal (Quebec), Ottawa (Ontario), and Halifax (Nova Scotia).

[Fig.](#page-5-0) 2 shows the share of electricity generation by fuel type, based on information from the Canada Energy Regulator [[48](#page-15-12)], for the three cities included in this study. In Quebec and Ontario, the electricity is generated mainly from renewable and non-fossil fuel energy sources: about 94 % of electricity is generated by hydropower in Quebec, about 59 % by nuclear power plants, and 24 % by hydropower in Ontario. In Nova Scotia, most of the electricity is generated by fossil fuels: 52 % from coal and coke, and 22 % from natural gas.
In Quebec, electricity generation predominantly relies on renewable sources, with hydropower accounting for 94 % and wind power contributing 5 %. However, the electrification of society, including the transportation sector, could potentially lead to increased electricity demand in the coming decades. Quebec currently stands as one of the Canadian provinces with the least energyrelated GHG emissions. As reported by CER [[49]](#page-15-13), the GHG intensity of Quebec's electricity grid was 0.0015 kgCO2eq/kWh of electricity generated in 2020. However, this value does not include other impacts such as biogenic decay in hydro reservoirs (rotting vegetation emitting CO^(2) and Methane (CH4)) and emissions related to transmission processes. In this study, we considered the value of 0.01023 kgCO2eq/kWh, sourced from OneClick LCA [[39]](#page-15-3) and Athena's Transparency Document (2019). This value was calculated based on data from the Ecoinvent 3.4 [[50](#page-15-14)] databases and incorporates all carbon emissions up to the final point of consumption.
Ontario is also a province that has its electricity generation mostly based on non-fossil sources. As reported by CER [[51]](#page-15-15), the GHG intensity of Ontario's electricity grid was 0.025 kgCO2eq/kWh of electricity generated in 2020. Similar to the case of Quebec, this value only reflects the emissions at the power plants. Therefore, in this study, we used the value of 0.028 kgCO2eq/kWh of electricity considered at the final point of consumption. This value was obtained from calculations based on Ecoinvent databases, sourced from OneClick LCA [[39](#page-15-3)] and Athena's Transparency Document [[52](#page-15-16)].
Nova Scotia has a totally different electricity grid profile, which relies mostly on fossil fuels. As reported by CER [[53]](#page-15-17), the GHG intensity of Nova Scotia's electricity grid was 0.670 kgCO2eq/kWh of electricity generated in 2020. We used a slightly higher value of 0.680 kgCO2eq/kWh, incorporating all carbon emissions up to the final point of consumption, based on the OneClick LCA [[39](#page-15-3)] and the Ecoinvent database [[50](#page-15-14)]. Due to the different grid mixes, the use of electricity in Nova Scotia generates 65 times more GHG emissions than in Quebec, and 24 times more than in Ontario. Although the use of natural gas is significantly intense in GHG emissions, it can be considered as an option for places dependent on coal, like Nova Scotia. The amount of CO₂ emitted in the production of 1 kWh of electricity using coal versus natural gas can vary based on several factors, including the efficiency of the power plants, the type of coal or natural gas being used, and the technology in place. On average, based on EIA [[54]](#page-15-18), coal-fired power plants emit around 1.025 kgCO₂eq/kWh of electricity generated, while natural gas-fired power plants are generally more efficient, ranging from 0.180 kgCO2eq/kWh [[55]](#page-15-19) to 0.440 kgCO2eq/kWh [[54]](#page-15-18)). The factor of 10.55 kWh/m^(3) [[56]](#page-15-20) was employed to convert the energy provided by 1 m^(3) of natural gas to an energy equivalent value of electricity. In this study, we considered the GHG intensity of natural gas use equal to 0.218 kgCO2eq/kWh (equivalent to 2.30 kgCO2/m^(3) ), based on the OneClick LCA [[39](#page-15-3)] database.
#### **3.** **Results** **and** **discussion**
This section presents the case study results for each location (Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax), followed by a discussion regarding each retrofit step. For each design improvement, at each location, the results include the annual energy consumption (in kWh/year), and total GHG emissions (in kgCO2eq) over a 20-year life cycle. Results are presented for Montreal first [(Table](#page-6-0) 4) and followed by Ottawa ([Table](#page-6-1) 6) and Nova Scotia ([Table](#page-10-0) 10). A comparative analysis between cities is provided at the end of this section.

- 3. **Upgrading** **building** **envelope**: adding additional insulation in the exterior walls and roofs and new roofing membrane and air barriers where necessary resulted in a reduction in total energy consumption, from 151,201 to 125,535 kWh/year, primarily due to a decrease in space heating demand, from 112,062 to 87,093 kWh/year. The operational emissions dropped from 30,948 to 25,694 kgCO2eq, while embodied emissions increased from 34,916 to 75,208 kgCO2eq. This indicates that the embodied emissions associated with manufacturing the new insulation materials, air barriers, and roofing membranes (i.e., 26,621 kgCO2eq from XPS, 8359 kgCO2eq from mineral wool, 1621 kgCO2eq from air barrier, and 3988 kgCO2eq from the roofing membrane [(Table](#page-4-3) 3) outweighed the reduction in operational emissions (5254 kgCO2eq). - 4. **Improving** **building** **airtightness**: The air infiltration rate of 3.9 ACH^(50) (air changes per hour, measured at a pressure differential of 50 Pa) was reduced to 2.0 ACH50. Although this value is not as low as the 0.6 ACH^(50) recommended in Passive House [[57](#page-15-21)]) certifications, we aimed at a more conservative retrofit scenario. The air infiltration requirements outlined, for example, in Quebec's energy transition program Novoclimat [[58]](#page-15-22) recommends a maximum value of 1.5 ACH^(50) for new buildings, while the Ontario Building Code [[59](#page-15-23)] suggests 2.5 ACH^(50) for homes. Similarly, standards like Energy Star [[60]](#page-15-24) specify the maximum air infiltration rate between 2.5 and 3.0 ACH50. In light of these considerations and variations in workmanship, we selected the value of 2.0 ACH^(50) to represent the improved airtightness. The improvement in the building's airtightness resulted in a reduction of annual energy consumption from 125,535 to 104,930 kWh/year and total GHG emissions reduction from 100,902 to 96,685 kgCO2eq due to the reduction of operational energy use emissions. Embodied emissions remained unchanged from the previous stage, as no new materials or equipment were added to this improvement. - 5 **Upgrading** **Windows** **and** **adding** **interior** **and** **exterior** **shading**: The previous double (clear) glazing was upgraded to a double low-E coated Argon-filled glazing unit, with a lower solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) and lower U-values (see [Table](#page-4-1) [2)](#page-4-1). The improvements in local shading were achieved through the substitution of conventional blinds with low-reflectance, high-transmittance shade rolls, which helped reduce lighting use and heating loads. The installation of overhangs above the windows' heads was implemented to avoid overheating during the summer season since the school building does not have a cooling system. This set of improvements led to a substantial decrease in overall energy consumption from 104,930 to 55,875 kWh/year. This reduction is attributed to both a 50 % drop in energy use for space heating (from 66,489 to 33,807 kWh/year), and a reduction in interior lighting usage (from 26,736 to 10,362 kWh/year). However, the total emissions still increased (from 96,685 to 166,416 kgCO2eq) primarily attributed to the embodied emissions associated with the production of new aluminum windows (i.e., 67,148 kgCO2eq, see [Table](#page-6-0) 4) and overhangs (12,623 kgCO2eq, see [Table](#page-4-3) 3). On the other hand, the reduction of operational emissions only offset 10,141 kgCO2eq (from 21,477 to 11,436 kgCO2eq). - 6. **Adding** **mechanical** **ventilation** **and** **heat** **recovery** **system**: To meet [[45]](#page-15-9) requirements, a mechanical ventilation system was added, replacing the previous reliance solely on natural ventilation in the old building. The mechanical ventilation system was designed to operate based on a minimum fresh air supply of 7.5 L/s/person as outlined in [Table](#page-4-0) 1. Additionally, a heat recovery system was added, with a heat recovery effectiveness of 0.70. The introduction of the mechanical ventilation system initially led to an increase in total energy use from 55,875 to 104,448 kWh/year. However, with the addition of heat recovery, the energy use decreased substantially from 104,448 to 75,310 kWh/year. The total emissions increased from 166,416 to 183,348 kgCO2eq (without the heat recovery) but decreased with the addition of the heat recovery from 183,348 to 177,393 kgCO2eq.
As shown in [Table](#page-6-2) 5, the 'baseline (a)' represents the existing school building, which uses natural gas for space heating. The 'baseline (b)' shares the same envelope characteristics, with the exception of the gas heating system being replaced by an electric heating

These two scenarios were compared with the final design, labeled as 'full retrofit (c)', which incorporates all the retrofit improvements previously mentioned in section [2.2.](#page-3-1) From the baseline (a) to the full retrofit (c), there is a reduction of 113,204 kWh/ year in total energy use, primarily in the energy use for space heating, attributed to the improvements made to the building envelope and installation of electric heating. Meanwhile, the total emissions decreased by 482,100 kgCO2eq, (a 73 % reduction), notably due to the reduction in operational emissions (a 98 % reduction) attributed to the replacement of natural gas with electric heating. As discussed in previous sections, Quebec's electricity grid is based on hydropower, which is a low-carbon source (i.e., 0.01023 kgCO2eq/ kWh), while the use of natural gas for heating has about 20 times higher GHG emission (i.e., 0.218 kgCO2eq/kWh). As a result, the transition from (a) to (c) yields reductions of the operational emissions that outweigh any potential increases in embodied emissions associated with the production of materials and equipment.
However, when examining the transition from (b) to (c), where the pre-retrofit design already includes electric heating, the conclusions are significantly different. There is a reduction of 75,850 kWh/year (60 %) in total energy use and operational emission reduction by 50 % associated with building envelope improvements and, while an increase of 111,826 kgCO2eq (by 170 %) is observed. Since the baseline (b) already uses electric heating, the reduction of operational emissions (by 50 %) is unable to offset the embodied emissions from adding new materials and equipment. In this context, the decision to undertake a retrofit may not appear justified solely from a GHG emission perspective. Nevertheless, its viability remains valid considering the potential reduction in electricity demand derived from energy efficiency, as well as the financial savings and improved user comfort. Further improvement could focus on retrofitting building envelope with low-carbon materials.

From (a) to (b), where the full retrofit included the replacement of natural gas heating with an electric heating system, the total annual energy use was reduced by 114,717 kWh/year, (62 %), resulting in the operational emission reduction by 18 %, while the total life cycle GHG emissions were reduced by 46,090 kgCO2eq over 20 years, 4 %. However, the transition from (a) to (c) yielded even more favorable outcomes. While the reduction in total annual energy consumption was slightly lower (i.e., 104,773 kWh/year v.s. 114,717 kWh/year, 56 %) due to the thermal efficiency of the natural gas heating system versus the COP = 1 considered for electric heating, the operational emission reduction by 38 % and the total GHG emission reduction achieved from (a) to (c) (i.e., 313,004 kgCO2eq) is approximately seven times greater than those from (a) to (b) (i.e., 46,090 kgCO2eq). The primary driver behind this improvement was the reduction of operational emissions, as the use of natural gas for space heating has a lower carbon footprint than relying on gridpurchased electricity in Nova Scotia. Furthermore, the shift from (a) to (c) also resulted in reduced embodied emissions, as the electric heating equipment was not added to the design.
In summary, the results show that all retrofit scenarios for Halifax (Nova Scotia) offered benefits in both reducing total annual energy consumption and overall life cycle GHG emissions with the natural gas heating scenario yielding lower environmental impact. These findings indicate that the decision to undertake this retrofit in Nova Scotia can be justified from both energy and GHG emissions perspectives.

# **4.** **Conclusions**
This paper presented the case study of a school building retrofit and used energy simulations and life cycle assessment tools to evaluate whether the reduction of operational emissions resulting from retrofit solutions can outweigh the embodied emissions tied to the new building envelopes and HVAC equipment. The analysis was carried out at three locations, i.e., Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, having similar climatic conditions but different electricity-grid profiles. The key findings include:
- **Impact** **of** **grid** **electricity** **source:** Building energy retrofit outcomes vary significantly depending on the electricity grid profile of the location. In regions where grid electricity relies heavily on fossil fuels (e.g., Nova Scotia), energy retrofits can effectively reduce both energy consumption and life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Conversely, in areas with a non-fossil fuel-based electricity supply (e.g., Quebec and Ontario), the embodied emissions from new materials and equipment may outweigh the operational emissions savings due to the energy efficiency improvement, particularly if the buildings already use electric heating. - **Potential** **of** **energy** **retrofits** **in** **GHG** **emission** **reduction:** While retrofits promote energy efficiency and reduce operational energy use and operational carbon emissions, the level of benefits achieved for their implementation from a carbon emissions perspective varies with the local energy mix. o In Montreal and Ottawa, retrofitting to electric heating and improving envelopes could cut operational emissions by up to 98 % and the total life cycle GHG emissions by up to 75 %. The shift from natural gas heating was the primary driver for the life cycle emissions reduction. However, if buildings already use electric heating, the reduction in operational emissions is unable to outweigh the embodied emissions associated with adding new materials and HVAC systems incorporated through the retrofits. The total life cycle emissions increased by +170 % for Montreal and by +56 % for Ottawa, respectively, for the electric-heated building.
oFor Halifax, where the grid-purchased electricity is generated primarily from fossil fuels, retrofitting to electric heating and improving envelopes can only reduce the total emissions by 4 % compared to 75 % in Montreal and Ottawa. This is due to the much less reduction in operational emissions by switching space heating from natural gas to electricity, only achieved 18 % compared to 94 % for Ottawa and 98 % for Montreal. The total life cycle GHG emissions can be reduced by 27 % when retaining the natural gas system for space heating due to an increased reduction in operational emission to 38 %. The results indicate that for places with electricity grid heavily from fossil fuel sources, energy efficiency retrofits are beneficial but switching building operations to all-electric may not be from a carbon perspective until the grid becomes cleaner.
oThe general conclusion is consistent with existing literature: the contribution of building energy retrofits to reducing the life cycle carbon emission is reduced when the embodied carbon associated with adding materials and equipment is accounted for,

• **Carbon** **Neutral** **Policies**: The study highlights the need for comprehensive carbon-neutral policies that consider both the building stock and the electricity grid's makeup. This approach is essential to maximize the spatial impact and effectiveness of decarbonization efforts.
oThe development of energy-efficient buildings is valid in any context. In this specific scenario of Quebec and Ontario, the decision to undertake a retrofit cannot be justified solely from a carbon perspective. With the increase in electricity demand due to the transition to electric vehicles, electrification of society, and global population increase, which may pressure the reintroduction of non-renewable sources to meet the increased demand for electricity, improving energy efficiency to reduce energy consumption is important.
oThese analyses provide insights highlighting the importance of a complete whole building life cycle GHG emission analysis including the local electricity grid profile for policymaking and performing LCA-based optimization considering both embodied and operational emissions in the design and operation of buildings. When the operational energy and emissions are significantly reduced due to a cleaner electricity grid and higher energy efficiency, reducing the embodied emission in developing retrofit strategies to achieve carbon-neutral buildings becomes important. Efforts should be made to low-carbon building materials and low-carbon building envelope retrofit solutions.
Although the conclusions are only based on this specific design, with limited information about the LCA database for local materials or future scenarios of electricity generation, this paper shows that the Carbon Neutral policies applied to a large territory, province, or country should be developed by considering the whole system composed of buildings and electricity grid. Otherwise, the success of a few Carbon carbon-neutral buildings will have a limited spatial impact, probably at additional costs, but will not contribute to the larger scope of complete decarbonization.
Limitations of the current study include:
- **Limited** **LCA** **data** **for** **local** **materials** **and** **equipment** to accurately represent the existing design specifications. For instance, there are few options for heating equipment and fenestration systems. While the impact on final results may be minimal, different brands and products have varying values of embodied emissions. The ones selected for this case study were the closest industry-available options to represent the existing design. - **Static** **energy** **consumption** **analysis** **and** **electricity** **grid** **profiles:** The energy consumption analysis was carried out over the typical metrological year and kept constant over the 20-year period. The LCA analysis assumes constant GHG intensity for electricity grids over 20 years, not accounting for potential changes in grid compositions due to technological advances or policy changes. - **Generalizability** **of** **findings:** Results are based on specific case scenarios and designs, which may not be universally applicable across different regions or building types.
To determine the optimal retrofit strategies based on local energy mixes, the framework presented in this study can be expanded in future studies:
- **Expansion** **of** **study** **regions** **and** **future** **energy** **scenarios:** Future studies should include a broader range of geographic locations and consider varying future electricity grid profiles by incorporating projections about emerging technologies and their impact on electricity demand and grid compositions to enhance the applicability and relevance of findings. The energy consumption over time considering the future climates should be also included. - **Integrating** **lifecycle** **cost** **analysis:** Life cycle cost analysis will be included to evaluate the economic benefits of retrofit strategies alongside the environmental impacts. Our future objectives include pursuing the development of a guideline for building design that takes into account the electricity grid profile, total life cycle carbon emissions, and the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) with respect to various geographic locations. - **Development** **of** **low-carbon** **building** **envelope** **solutions:** There is a need for focused research on low-carbon building materials and building envelope retrofit solutions to further reduce embodied emissions in the pursuit of achieving carbonneutral buildings.
